extracted.intended_audience: stakeholders commenting on or implementing DHS public charge rule (immigration practitioners, advocates, state and local officials, agency adjudicators)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and interpretive criteria DHS uses to define and implement the public charge ground of inadmissibility, including scope, evidentiary and interpretive approaches, procedural commitments (notice-and-comment, guidance, training), and measures to mitigate chilling effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory scope of public charge ground
rubrics_metrics.description: The public charge ground of inadmissibility applies to applicants for visas, admission, and adjustment of status as established by Congress; DHS must apply that ground to all noncitizens seeking admission or adjustment of status unless otherwise expressly exempted by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes it lacks authority to change the statutory existence or structure of the public charge ground and must apply the ground where Congress has directed; procedural comments about litigation or policy preferences to amend the statute are outside DHS's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: DHS authority to define 'likely at any time to become a public charge'
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Congress enacted the ground without defining 'public charge' or 'likely at any time to become a public charge,' Congress authorized agencies administering the ground to determine and specify what those terms mean and how inadmissibility determinations will be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS may provide definitions and implementation guidance (including what benefits are considered) consistent with statute and case law; the rule should reflect a permissible, faithful implementation of the statutory standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive standard: forward-looking subjective aspect and totality of the circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule provides a close connection to statutory language and reflects the forward-looking subjective aspect of the statutory standard, evaluating each noncitizen 'in the totality of the circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators should apply a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis with attention to forward-looking likelihood rather than rigid numerical thresholds; this is DHS's chosen interpretive frame as consistent with the INA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of dependence criterion (primary dependence vs. duration thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS explained why the degree of dependence that would give rise to inadmissibility under this rule—'primary dependence on the government for subsistence'—is a more sound interpretation than the 2019 Rule's reliance-on-benefits-over-a-duration threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule favors assessing primary dependence for subsistence as the relevant degree of dependence indicative of a public charge, rather than counting benefit receipt over time or relying on duration-based thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow list of public benefits considered
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider a narrower list of public benefits for the purposes of public charge determinations than the 2019 Final Rule, excluding many programs (for example, DHS proposed not to include SNAP benefits and most Medicaid benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS consulted benefits-granting agencies (HHS, USDA) and relies on their descriptions to determine which benefits are indicative of primary dependence; benefits not indicative of such dependence are generally excluded from consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between inadmissibility determinations and benefit eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: This final rule does not govern eligibility for public benefits; it governs the determination of whether an applicant for admission or adjustment of status is likely at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies or comments about broad eligibility for public benefits are outside the rule's scope; the rule should avoid being read as changing who is eligible to apply for or receive benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on application to extensions of stay and change of status
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS cannot apply the public charge ground of inadmissibility to requests for extension of stay or change of status because the statutory ground applies only to applications for a visa, admission, and adjustment of status under the INA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS declines to impose conditions related to public benefits on extension-of-stay or change-of-status petitions; statutory text controls scope of applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of existing nonimmigrant controls and self-reliance requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns about noncitizens' self-reliance in extension/change contexts are often addressed by existing statutory/regulatory requirements (e.g., employer wage requirements for certain work visas, students' proof of funds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many nonimmigrant categories are barred from receiving the benefits considered by this rule, DHS views additional conditions on extensions/changes as unnecessary for those categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural sufficiency and notice-and-comment opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS has completed multiple rounds of notice-and-comment (including an ANPRM, virtual listening sessions, and the NPRM) and asserts that this rulemaking process provided ample opportunity for public participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments arguing for delay of issuance pending litigation are, in DHS's view, unwarranted where robust notice-and-comment has occurred; agencies should document the notice-and-comment steps taken when defending process adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide reasoned analysis for departures from prior rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency adopts an approach different from a prior administration's rule, the agency must include justification and reasoning for the approaches taken; proposed rules must explain why the agency opted for a different approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS documents where the new rule substantively differs from the 2019 Final Rule and explains why it opted for alternative interpretations (e.g., dependence standard, narrower benefits list); failure to provide reasoned analysis can be characterized as arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and mitigation of chilling effects
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS acknowledges that prior public charge policies (notably the 2019 Final Rule) had significant chilling effects—deterring eligible individuals from enrolling in benefits—and that these collateral effects should be considered and mitigated in fashioning the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule design should weigh evidence of chilling effects, avoid features that unduly discourage benefit use, and include commitments to clear, comprehensible guidance to minimize fear and confusion among noncitizens and families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based consideration of collateral effects
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS reviews and acknowledges studies and data showing disenrollment and reduced participation in programs (Medicaid, SNAP, CHIP, WIC) and recognizes methodological variation across studies; DHS took such evidence into account in crafting the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should consider differing methodologies and estimates, document the evidence considered, and explain how the evidence informed policy choices (e.g., excluding certain benefits from consideration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public health and emergency context consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated chilling effects and demonstrated that pandemics are not hypothetical; policy should account for the possibility of similar occurrences in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking should take into account how emergency public-health contexts affect vulnerable populations and access to benefits, and design measures to avoid undermining public health (e.g., avoid discouraging vaccination/testing/treatment-seeking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational feasibility and minimization of paperwork burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2019 Final Rule imposed heavy paperwork burdens (e.g., Form I-944) and complexity; DHS aims to minimize unnecessary information collection and avoid imposing undue burdens on applicants and employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rules to be administrable and comprehensible for service providers and applicants; avoid overly complex formulas or layered evidence requirements that are difficult to apply or understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of discretionary public charge bonds for adjustment applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS acknowledges its statutory discretionary authority under INA section 213 to consider public charge bonds for adjustment applicants inadmissible only under section 212(a)(4), and will include provisions to offer bonds in its discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When USCIS chooses to offer an adjustment applicant the opportunity to submit a public charge bond, USCIS will set the bond amount at no less than $1,000, provide submission instructions, amend related regulations, and provide guidance/training to officers to ensure fair, consistent exercise of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to officer guidance, training, and consistent adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS will provide officers with guidance and training to ensure discretionary authorities (including bonds and public charge determinations) are exercised in a fair, efficient, and consistent manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear guidance and training are presented as necessary to mitigate unequal treatment and to make determinations clear and comprehensible to officers and applicants; DHS commits to issuing such guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability of rule provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS intends that the provisions of the rule be treated as severable to the maximum extent possible so that if any provision is deemed invalid, other parts will remain in effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft rules with severability clauses and consider modular design so valid provisions can remain operational if others are invalidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of family unity and collateral harms while applying individual inadmissibility standard
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS appreciates concerns about family unity and collateral harms (e.g., impacts on U.S. citizen children), but notes that the potential for a portion of a family to be deemed inadmissible is inherent in an individual inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While individual determinations are required, agencies should consider collateral effects in policy design (e.g., by narrowing benefits considered and mitigating chilling effects) to avoid unnecessary harm to families.
